title: Mutations and gene editing
summary: How changes to the base sequence of genes arise, how substitutions, insertions and deletions affect polypeptides, and why mutation is the source of genetic variation.

keyterms.definition: A structural change to a gene at the molecular level: a change in its base sequence by substitution, insertion or deletion.
Mutation in which one base in a gene is replaced by a different base; it may change one amino acid or none.
A position in the genome where individuals differ by one base, resulting from a base substitution mutation.
Mutation in which one or more extra nucleotides are added to a gene's base sequence.
Mutation in which one or more nucleotides are removed from a gene's base sequence.
Change in the reading frame caused by inserting or deleting a number of bases that is not a multiple of three, altering all following codons.
Mutation that changes an amino acid codon into a stop codon, so translation ends early and the polypeptide is shortened.
An agent that increases the mutation rate, such as mutagenic chemicals or high-energy radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays).
Mutation in a cell that gives rise to gametes; it can be passed on to offspring.
Mutation in a body cell; it is passed only to that cell's descendants by mitosis, not to offspring, and may contribute to cancer.
Differences in alleles between individuals; mutation is the original source of new alleles, on which natural selection acts.
Technique for investigating a gene's function by altering it so that it no longer works and observing the effect on the organism.
Gene-editing system derived from bacterial antiviral defence: a guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at a chosen target sequence.
RNA with a sequence complementary to the target DNA; it binds Cas9 and base-pairs with the target so Cas9 cuts there.
Base sequence that is identical or very similar across species, explained by functional constraint (selection against change) or slower mutation rates.

options: A change in the number of chromosomes in a cell
A change in the base sequence of a gene
A change in which genes are being transcribed
A new combination of alleles produced by meiosis
questions.explanation: A gene mutation is a structural change at the molecular level: bases substituted, inserted or deleted. Changes in chromosome number (e.g. non-disjunction) and new allele combinations from meiosis are different processes.

questions.prompt: Match each type of mutation to its description.

pairs.right: One base replaced by a different base
One or more extra nucleotides added
All codons after the mutation are read differently

questions.explanation: Substitutions swap one base; insertions and deletions change the length of the sequence and, unless a multiple of three bases is involved, shift the reading frame.

questions.statement: A base substitution always changes the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide.
questions.explanation: Because the genetic code is degenerate, the new codon may code for the same amino acid (a silent mutation). Substitutions can also change one amino acid or create a stop codon.

questions.text: A position where individuals differ by a single base, resulting from a base substitution, is called a single-nucleotide ___.
questions.explanation: SNPs arise from base substitutions; because of degeneracy, an SNP within a gene may or may not change one amino acid in the polypeptide.

questions.prompt: A substitution changes the mRNA codon UUU to UUC. Both codons code for phenylalanine. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
options: Phenylalanine is replaced by a different amino acid
The polypeptide is shortened
All amino acids after this point are changed
No change in the amino acid sequence
questions.explanation: UUC still codes for phenylalanine, so the polypeptide is unchanged. This is possible because the genetic code is degenerate.

questions.prompt: Why is insertion of a single nucleotide near the start of a gene usually more harmful than a single base substitution?
options: It shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it
Insertions always produce a stop codon immediately
Insertions occur in introns, which are then translated
Insertions prevent the gene from being transcribed
questions.explanation: Codons are read in threes from a fixed start, so one extra base changes all downstream codons. The polypeptide is very different and a premature stop codon often appears, so it is unlikely to function.

questions.statement: Deleting three consecutive nucleotides from a gene does not cause a frameshift.
questions.explanation: Removing three bases removes one codon's worth, so the reading frame after it is restored; the polypeptide typically loses one amino acid. An example is the loss of one phenylalanine from the CFTR protein in most cases of cystic fibrosis.

questions.text: A mutation that changes an amino acid codon into a stop codon, producing a shortened polypeptide, is called a ___ mutation.
questions.explanation: A stop codon ends translation early, so the polypeptide is truncated and usually non-functional. A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged; a missense mutation swaps one amino acid.

questions.prompt: Put the consequences of a base substitution in a gene in order.
items: The base sequence of the gene is altered
The transcribed mRNA contains an altered codon
A different amino acid is added during translation
The polypeptide folds differently and its function may change
questions.explanation: A change in DNA is carried through transcription into the mRNA codon, then through translation into the amino acid sequence, which determines how the protein folds and works (as in sickle cell anaemia).

questions.prompt: Which mutation is most likely to have the least effect on the polypeptide?
options: Deletion of one base near the start of the gene
Substitution that creates a stop codon near the start
Substitution of the third base of a codon
Insertion of one base near the start of the gene
questions.explanation: Many codons for the same amino acid differ only in their third base, so a third-position substitution is often silent. Single-base insertions/deletions cause frameshifts, and early stop codons truncate the polypeptide.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a mutagen?
options: Visible light
Radio waves
Short-wavelength ultraviolet radiation
Infrared radiation
questions.explanation: High-energy, short-wavelength radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays) can damage DNA and so increase the mutation rate. Low-energy, long-wavelength radiation does not have enough energy to do this.

questions.statement: Mutations can occur anywhere in the base sequence of a genome, although some bases have a higher probability of mutating than others.
questions.explanation: Mutation is random in the sense that any base can change, but probabilities are not exactly equal across the genome; some sites mutate more often.

questions.statement: Bacteria exposed to an antibiotic deliberately mutate the specific base needed to become resistant.
questions.explanation: There is no natural mechanism for making a particular mutation to suit a need. Resistance mutations arise randomly; the antibiotic then selects bacteria that already carry them.

questions.text: Chemicals such as benzopyrene in tobacco smoke, which increase the rate of mutation, are called ___.
questions.explanation: Mutagens are agents that raise the mutation rate; they include certain chemicals and high-energy radiation. Pathogens cause disease and antigens trigger immune responses.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to its likely consequence.

pairs.left: Mutation in a cell that produces gametes

pairs.right: Passed only to daughter cells by mitosis
A mutation arising without any mutagen

questions.explanation: Only germ-cell mutations reach the next generation. Somatic mutations affect the individual and its cell lineage, and can contribute to cancer. Copying errors cause mutations even without mutagens.

questions.prompt: Why is mutation described as the original source of genetic variation?
options: Mutations always increase an organism's fitness
Meiosis and fertilisation can only reshuffle existing alleles, while mutation creates new ones
Mutation is the only process that changes allele frequencies
Mutations occur only when the environment changes
questions.explanation: Crossing over, random orientation and fertilisation create new combinations of alleles, but only mutation produces new alleles. Natural selection then acts on this variation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the effects of mutations is correct?
options: Most mutations are beneficial
All mutations cause genetic disease
Mutations in somatic cells are passed to offspring
Most mutations are neutral or harmful, and only a few are beneficial
questions.explanation: A random change to a functioning gene is more likely to disrupt it than improve it, and many changes have no effect. Rare beneficial mutations are what natural selection can favour.

questions.text: Mutations in ___ cells are not passed on to offspring.
questions.explanation: Somatic (body) cells do not produce gametes, so their mutations stay within the individual. Mutations in germ cells, gametes or the zygote can be inherited.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a mutation can contribute to evolution.
items: A random mutation in a germ cell creates a new allele
The allele is passed to offspring in a gamete
Individuals with the allele survive and reproduce more if it is beneficial
The allele's frequency in the gene pool increases over generations
questions.explanation: Mutation supplies new alleles; inheritance through gametes keeps them in the population; natural selection then changes allele frequencies, which is evolution.

questions.statement: Errors during DNA replication can cause mutations even without exposure to mutagens.
questions.explanation: Occasionally a wrong nucleotide is inserted and not corrected, or DNA repair makes a mistake. Mutagens raise the mutation rate but are not required for mutation.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a gene knockout?
options: To make a gene inoperative and observe the effect, revealing the gene's function
To insert a gene from another species to improve a crop
To increase the rate of transcription of a gene
To remove all mutations from an organism's genome
questions.explanation: If a gene is made non-functional and the organism changes (e.g. lacks a structure or enzyme), the difference shows what the gene normally does.

questions.text: In CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, a ___ RNA complementary to the target sequence directs Cas9 to the correct site.
questions.explanation: The guide RNA base-pairs with the target DNA, so Cas9 cuts only at that sequence. Changing the guide RNA's sequence retargets the system to any gene.

questions.statement: CRISPR sequences and Cas9 evolved in prokaryotes as a defence against viruses.
questions.explanation: Bacteria store short viral DNA sequences in CRISPR arrays; RNA copies of these guide Cas proteins to cut the DNA of the same virus if it infects again. Scientists adapted this system for gene editing.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of editing a gene with CRISPR–Cas9 in order.
items: A guide RNA is designed to be complementary to the target sequence
Cas9 and the guide RNA are introduced into the cell
The guide RNA base-pairs with the target DNA
Cas9 cuts both strands of the DNA at the target
The cell repairs the break, altering the gene's sequence
questions.explanation: Targeting depends on complementary base pairing between guide RNA and DNA; Cas9 then makes a double-strand cut. Repair can insert or delete bases (knocking the gene out) or copy in a supplied sequence.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Enzyme that cuts both DNA strands
Base-pairs with the target DNA sequence
Stores sequences from viral DNA in bacteria
Has a gene deliberately made inoperative

questions.explanation: In bacteria, CRISPR arrays remember past viral infections and Cas9 destroys viral DNA. In the lab the same tools can knock out genes to study their function.

questions.prompt: Some genes have almost identical base sequences in very distantly related species. Which hypothesis best explains this?
options: Mutations never occur in essential genes
Changes would impair an essential function, so natural selection removes them
These genes are not transcribed, so they cannot change
The species recently shared a common ancestor
questions.explanation: If a protein's function is vital, almost any change is harmful and individuals carrying it are selected against, so the sequence stays conserved. Mutations do still occur in these genes.

questions.statement: One hypothesis for highly conserved sequences is that they have a slower mutation rate than other parts of the genome.
questions.explanation: Two hypotheses are considered: functional requirement (selection against changes) and slower rates of mutation in those sequences. They are not mutually exclusive.

questions.text: A library of ___ organisms, each with a different gene inactivated, can be used to study gene function.
questions.explanation: Researchers keep collections of knockout lines (e.g. of model organisms) so the effect of losing each gene can be compared. Transgenic organisms have gained a gene rather than lost one.

questions.prompt: Why must the guide RNA be complementary to the target sequence?
options: So that it can be translated into Cas9
So that it can replace the damaged section of DNA
So that it binds only at the target site, making Cas9 cut there and nowhere else
So that it can activate transcription of the target gene
questions.explanation: Specific base pairing between guide RNA and DNA gives CRISPR–Cas9 its precision. The guide RNA is not translated and does not itself become part of the DNA.

questions.statement: Cas9 cuts only one strand of the DNA double helix at the target site.
questions.explanation: Cas9 makes a double-strand break. When the cell repairs this break, bases are often inserted or deleted, which is one way a gene can be knocked out.
